papers.title: Causal graph fusion across incomplete cohorts and causal steering of tabular foundation models
papers.abstract: Clinical data are split across incomplete cohorts with partially overlapping variables. Causal discovery under missing data and multi-source integration have developed separately, and tabular foundation models cannot take a causal graph without retraining. We make two contributions. First, causal graph fusion learns a partial ancestral graph on the shared variables, fuses it into each cohort's graph under temporal background knowledge and lets Markov blankets guide re-imputation, so missing data are handled inside discovery. Second, causal attention steering compiles the learned graph into the attention of a frozen tabular foundation model at inference. Against known ground truth, fusion dominates pooled and per-cohort baselines in every missingness and heterogeneity condition tested (p<0.001), and steering improves discrimination under distribution shift (p<10^{-5}), a gain that a random graph does not produce. In two spinal cord injury cohorts, fusion orients age, albumin and hemoglobin as ancestors of length of stay, a set no single cohort orients in full, and yields compact, temporally ordered predictor sets that match or exceed automatic feature selection on four of five outcomes.

papers.title: The Cost of Coverage: Conformalising Native Forecast Uncertainty for GB Wind Power
papers.abstract: Uncertainty bands on wind forecasts help inform reserve sizing and commitments, but often fail to deliver their stated coverage. We apply conformal prediction to native bands to see what it adds and what it costs, comparing six forecasters, from ARIMA to a tabular foundation model, at two wind farms in Great Britain (GB) under operational conditions. We show that calibration repairs empirical marginal coverage with little or no Winkler Score penalty, but this apparent success conceals under-coverage in high winds. Calibrating by forecast wind regime turns marginal coverage into regime-level coverage, cutting day-ahead out-of-band volume in high winds by over 40% relative to pooled calibration while narrowing bands overall.

papers.title: Electoral Intelligence: A Neural Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial Model for Forecasting Swedish Municipal Elections
papers.abstract: Forecasting local elections is difficult because electoral competition is geographically heterogeneous, highly overdispersed, and characterized by many party-municipality combinations with little or no electoral activity. This article develops a bounded neural zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) model for forecasting party-level vote counts in Swedish municipal elections. The model combines a count component for expected votes, a zero-inflation component for structural electoral absence, municipality-specific dispersion, and learned embeddings capturing latent party, municipality, and party-municipality structure. Model training relies on data from the 2014, 2018, and 2022 Swedish municipal elections and performance is evaluated on a held-out set of municipalities. Testing results show strong predictive accuracy in both vote counts and vote shares. Explanatory diagnostics indicate that latent party structure, local party-municipality relationships, electoral persistence, organizational capacity, and candidate-electorate representational similarity are among the most important determinants of predictive performance. Following model evaluation and diagnostics, the selected specification is refit on all historical data and applied to generate forecasts for the 2026 municipal elections. The proposed framework provides a flexible approach for studying local electoral competition in multiparty systems characterized by heterogeneous party presence and substantial geographic variation.

papers.title: Online and Survey Representations of Well-Being: Coherence and Cross-Source Correspondence
papers.abstract: Digital traces may complement population surveys in the measurement of well-being, but the two sources do not necessarily capture identical constructs. We compare the Human Flourishing Geographic Index (HFGI) with World Values Survey and European Social Survey measures across three domains using structural equation models. The results show strong within-source coherence and construct-specific cross-source correspondence. Cross-source convergence varies across domains; the observed pattern is consistent with stronger correspondence where the underlying indicators are more closely aligned conceptually. Near-perfect agreement would be unexpected, since surveys elicit standardized self-reports, whereas HFGI captures naturally occurring public expressions. HFGI should therefore be viewed as a distinct but empirically connected measurement system that complements survey-based evidence on well-being.

papers.title: Beyond the Lower-Star Filtration: Alternative Filtration Methods for Persistent Homology
papers.abstract: In the lower-star filtration (LSF), simplices are assigned filtration values according to the maximum-vertex rule, with each simplex entering the filtration when its highest-valued vertex appears. A limitation of this construction is that some higher-dimensional simplices may enter simultaneously with their boundary faces, causing certain topological features to be filled immediately upon formation and thus not appear in the resulting persistence diagram. To address this limitation, we propose three alternative filtration methods: the \(\varepsilon\)-lower-star filtration (ELSF), the \(L_p\) filtration (LpF), and the softmax filtration (SMF). {ELSF introduces a dimension-dependent delay to the maximum-vertex rule,} allowing higher-dimensional simplices to enter the filtration after their boundary faces, whereas {LpF and SMF use aggregation functions that depend on all vertex values rather} than solely on their maximum. By modifying how filtration values are assigned, these methods allow simplices to enter the filtration more progressively, so that topological features such as loops and voids may persist over longer filtration intervals rather than being filled immediately. Consequently, the resulting persistence diagrams may include persistence features that are not observed under LSF, potentially providing useful information for distinguishing data populations. Experimental results on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed filtration methods are computationally efficient and can provide greater sensitivity to structural differences in the data than LSF.

papers.title: Sparse Network Inference under Imperfect Detection and its Application to Ecological Networks
papers.abstract: Recovering latent structure from count data has received considerable attention in network inference, particularly when one seeks both cross-group interactions and within-group similarity patterns in bipartite networks, which are widely used in ecology research. Such networks are often sparse and prone to imperfect detection. Existing models mainly focus on interaction recovery, while the induced similarity graphs are much less studied. Moreover, existing models for under-counted data place sparsity, if at all, on the detection model rather than on these graphs. To address these issues, we propose a nonnegative low-rank factorization framework that jointly estimates detection probabilities and promotes sparse within- and cross-group graphs through $\ell_{1/2}$ regularization. For the resulting nonconvex, nonsmooth problem, we develop an ADMM-based algorithm with adaptive penalization, and establish asymptotic feasibility and KKT stationarity of cluster points under stated assumptions. We also give sufficient conditions for exact recovery of within- and cross-group graphs. On synthetic data with up to 20% missing entries, the method recovers the graphs and detection probabilities with competitive accuracy. Across three ecological datasets, it matches the baseline held-out predictions while estimating detection probabilities and within- and cross-group graphs.

papers.title: Calibrated Order-Randomized Rosenblatt Tests
papers.abstract: We test whether a multivariate vector X conforms to a specified distribution F, as in copula modelling and density forecasting. The Rosenblatt transform reduces this to testing uniformity, but its arbitrary coordinate ordering affects power under dependence. We study order randomization: transforming under many random orderings and merging evidence with dependence-robust rules. Reordering only redistributes the Mahalanobis signal energy, so one ordering is a lucky or unlucky draw, and pooling raises calibrated power. We compare against two order-invariant baselines, the chi-squared energy test and the symmetric-root test. With F known, the e-value average over orderings is at least as powerful as the symmetric-root test in every setting we ran, and as the chi-squared test on concentrated and fully diffuse departures. With Gaussian mean and covariance estimated, the classical conditional probability integral transform keeps each ordering's p-values exact and e-values valid, a parametric bootstrap calibrates the pooled tests, and the comparisons hold except for deficits of at most 0.02 against the symmetric-root test on single-coordinate departures. Validating a Gaussian risk model for nine currencies, the test flags Brexit, COVID and other episodes; it extends to any null with computable, simulable conditionals.

papers.title: False Discovery Rate Control via Prediction-Based, Model-Agnostic Data Splitting: An Application to Gut Microbiome Data in Liver Function
papers.abstract: Many methods have been proposed to control the false discovery rate (FDR) in feature selection, yet challenges remain when the relationship between predictors and the outcome is complex. We propose a prediction-based data-splitting procedure that can leverage flexible predictive models while controlling the FDR. The data are divided into three parts: one for model training and two for constructing the mirror statistic. For each feature, we construct a negative control using the remaining features without incorporating outcome information and define a test statistic based on the resulting change in predictive performance. Under the null, such a perturbation is approximately equally likely to increase or decrease predictive performance, yielding a statistic symmetric about zero. In contrast, perturbing an informative feature tends to reduce predictive performance, resulting in a large positive statistic. Features are selected by thresholding these statistics, with false discoveries estimated from the corresponding negative tail to control the FDR. We apply the proposed method to liver function microbiome data, where high-dimensional, correlated features and potentially complex feature--outcome relationships make reliable type I error control particularly important for reproducible scientific discovery. Through simulation studies and the real-data application, we demonstrate that the proposed framework provides robust FDR control and can be integrated with state-of-the-art machine-learning models to accommodate complex relationships between features and the outcome.

papers.title: Dynamic Smart Charging Through Integrated Agent-based Simulation and Optimization Modeling
papers.abstract: Coordinated electric vehicle (EV) charging can improve alignment between transportation operations and power-system conditions as electrification expands. This study develops an integrated simulation-optimization framework that embeds demand-aware charging (DAC) and grid-responsive charging, including unidirectional smart charging (V1G) and vehicle-to-grid (V2G), within an agent-based model, enabling dynamic feedback between optimized vehicle (dis)charging decisions and evolving transportation-system states. Using the Austin 6-county region, the framework evaluates 15,000 shared autonomous electric vehicles (SAEVs) under DAC, V1G, fleet-only V2G, and combined fleet-plus-household V2G. Results show coordinated strategies concentrate charging toward midday and provide selective evening discharge while maintaining service performance. Under favorable pricing, V2G reduces net CO2 emissions from 45 kg/SAEV/day under DAC to below 40 kg and lowers emission intensity by up to 14% to 0.14 kg per vehicle-mile traveled. DAC and V1G offer near-term options, whereas high V2G costs may hinder adoption. Realized benefits depend on tariffs, vehicle availability, and V2G maturity.

papers.title: Snow Changes Drought Characterization but Not Drought Predictability: A Leakage-Free Multiscale Study in Ohio
papers.abstract: We examine whether accounting for snow accumulation and melt, which precipitation-based drought indices ignore, changes drought characterization and one-month-ahead drought forecasting at three stations in Ohio, USA (1953--2026). The Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) is compared with the Standardized Snow Melt and Rain Index (SMRI), and both are decomposed with the Haar maximal overlap discrete wavelet transform. Nonlinear autoregressive networks without (NAR) and with (NARX) wavelet inputs are compared over 100 paired repetitions in a leakage-free design (past-only wavelet inputs, untouched test period), together with persistence, climatology, and linear autoregressive benchmarks. Snow changes the 3-month index mainly from December to May (mean absolute SMRI--SPI differences of up to 0.17--0.28). These differences are attributable to the snow-adjusted input rather than to the fitted distribution, are robust to the snow-model parameters, and change the drought classification of 21--32\% of the December--May drought months. Wavelet inputs reduce NARX error relative to NAR by 6--10\% for the 3-month indices in 92--100\% of the repetitions, but not for the 6-month indices. A linear autoregression with 7--12 lags is at least as accurate as two-lag NARX for every series, and networks given six lags gain at most 4.5\% from the wavelet inputs and only match the autoregression. The forecast gain therefore reflects the memory of the accumulated index rather than multiscale information, and it is similar for the SPI and the SMRI. Snow matters for drought monitoring in winter and spring, but not for one-month predictability.

papers.title: Portfolio-aware scenario transfer of reserve movements: evidence from Lloyd's syndicates
papers.abstract: A claims-development movement on one portfolio may not transfer directly as a stress to another size. We estimate how to transfer such scenarios between portfolio sizes, using 632 syndicate-years from 117 Lloyd's syndicates over 2015-2024. The measured movement is the change in gross claims estimates on selected older underwriting cohorts, divided by opening gross claims outstanding plus reserves taken on in the year whose development it includes; it is not a pure measure of opening-reserve deterioration. Its dispersion falls materially with reserve size, and a size-based scale predicts held-out syndicates far better than a single market scale. But the transferred upper tail understates the smallest books: in the smallest reserve-size quartile, six of 158 held-out observations exceeded the transferred 99.5th percentile, against 0.79 expected, from three syndicates. Square-root scaling has descriptively lower held-out pinball loss at 99% and 99.5%, though more misses among the largest books. For a GBP 500m portfolio the transferred empirical 99.5th percentile is 0.34 of reserves (95% credible interval, conditional on the fitted model, 0.23-0.52), against 0.67 in the raw market pool. Both are Syndicate 5820's 2016 movement. The contribution is inspectable scenario comparability, not a calibrated capital quantile or a next-year forecast.

papers.title: From Point Anomalies to Anomalous Driving Episodes: Interpreting Abnormal Driving from Vehicle Telematics
papers.abstract: Vehicle telematics provides detailed observations of driving behaviour that can be useful for automobile insurance risk assessment. Existing approaches often summarize these data through counts of harsh events or individually unusual observations, although driving movements naturally develop over time. Building on a previously proposed hidden Markov model (HMM) framework that identifies pointwise anomalies, we identify short intervals in which a sequence of observations is unusual when considered together. We then examine the original acceleration signals to measure the magnitude and temporal concentration of these episodes and identify recurring patterns of vehicle movement. Temporal concentration describes whether acceleration activity is distributed evenly across an episode or concentrated in relatively few observations. Using a controlled telematics dataset containing normal, aggressive, and drowsy driving by the same drivers, we evaluate the proposed measures through comparisons matched by driver and road type. We find that statistical anomaly measures depend on the driving population used to train the HMM. More importantly, mean temporal concentration alone distinguishes normal from abnormal driving more effectively than the original pointwise anomaly indices across different reference populations. The recurring movement patterns further reveal different characteristics of abnormal driving, with stronger longitudinal acceleration during aggressive driving and more frequent lateral corrections or excursions during drowsy driving. The framework therefore goes beyond pointwise anomaly detection, providing interpretable behavioural features that can be calculated for unlabeled trips, used for trip-level assessment, aggregated across a driver's trip history, and subsequently evaluated alongside existing telematics and rating variables for insurance risk modelling and ratemaking.

papers.title: Bayesian Unit-level Quantile Modeling with Application to Wealth Data
papers.abstract: Modeling wealth quantiles over time and space and across fine-grained demographic classifications is of vital importance to policy makers. However, such data present unique challenges for standard small area estimation methodologies because they are highly skewed and heavy-tailed with both positive and negative values. Traditional area-level modeling and design-based approaches struggle to capture these features. Meanwhile, existing unit-level methodology frequently treats the survey design as ignorable and does not apply to surveys that are repeated over time. Often the analysis is restricted to alternative response variables that are non-negative, such as poverty indicators or income. To overcome these limitations, we propose a Bayesian, asymmetric Laplace pseudolikelihood model that is able to capture the major features of wealth while adjusting for survey weights and accounting for both spatial and temporal dependence. We present a Gibbs sampling algorithm for our model, as well as a variational Bayes algorithm for fast computation. We apply the method to the Survey of Income and Program Participation to characterize geographic, temporal, and demographic variation in the distribution of U.S. household wealth, including for sparsely sampled domains where direct estimates are unavailable or unstable.

papers.title: Competitive Balance Beyond Standings: Bayesian Inference for Latent Tiers and Structural Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Competitive balance has long been a central concern in sports economics, tied to outcome uncertainty, fan engagement, and the way leagues design their policies. Most existing measures of competitive balance are built from standings or winning percentages, which say little about how overall parity relates to the way teams sort into latent competitive tiers. We propose a Bayesian framework based on the Bradley-Terry model that jointly estimates the number of competitive tiers and team memberships. To capture the overall degree of competitive heterogeneity, we introduce a structural balance parameter defined on the unit interval within a hierarchical model, and we establish theoretical results giving this parameter a clear interpretation:it is directly tied to the separation between tiers, and overall heterogeneity depends on both the size and frequency of cross-tier differences. Importantly, structural balance is distinct from the information content of the schedule itself, so leagues with different numbers of teams and games can be compared on equal footing. Inference is carried out with an efficient posterior sampling algorithm that jointly handles team abilities, tier structure, home advantage, and structural balance. Simulation studies validate the proposed method, showing accurate recovery of the latent competitive structure and correct performance of the structural-balance testing procedure. Applied to the NBA and NFL, it reveals that the two leagues exhibit similar global structural balance despite very different competitive organizations: the NBA has three latent tiers, while the NFL has two broader ones, and the NFL's sparser schedule produces considerably more posterior uncertainty. Overall parity, it turns out, can mask quite different forms of competitive stratification-something standings-based measures alone cannot detect.

papers.title: Risk-set reconstruction balance: zero-targeted diagnostics for artificial censoring in clone-censor-weight analyses
papers.abstract: In clone-censor-weight (CCW) analyses, inverse probability of censoring weighting corrects selection from artificial censoring at protocol deviation. Balance diagnostics, such as the end-of-grace between-strategy standardised mean difference (SMD) and censoring balance, compare different populations, and their zero targets under a correct model are not formally stated. We show that, under positivity and a correct censoring model, the weighted retained individuals reconstruct the risk set before each censoring interval and the baseline population, and we propose risk-set reconstruction balance (RRB), which measures how far they depart from these two populations. Interval RRB has a zero target for every history function, including post-baseline covariates, for which between-strategy SMDs have none. Cumulative RRB keeps a zero target for baseline covariates after outcome events, whereas the end-of-grace SMD acquires a depletion term. In simulations, interval RRB responded to an omitted term's effect on censoring whether or not the term was prognostic. Under correct models, the exceedance rate of its studentised maximum over a null reference for chance imbalance was 3.5-6.0% (nominal 5%) when the censoring model pooled nine intervals and mostly 1.0-4.5% under censoring in a single interval. With many early events, cumulative RRB stayed near zero, whereas the end-of-grace SMD reached 0.40; under loss to follow-up that the weights ignored, cumulative RRB departed from zero and interval RRB stayed small. In a case study, interval RRB flagged a dispensing indicator outside the censoring model. Interval RRB checks the censoring model, and cumulative RRB the representation of the baseline population.

papers.title: Coherent forecast combination for linearly constrained multiple time series
papers.abstract: Forecasting linearly constrained multiple time series, as those arising in National Accounts, energy systems and supply chain planning, requires that the forecasts of all variables jointly satisfy the underlying accounting or resource-balance identities. When several experts provide forecasts for some or all of the variables, classical forecast combination operates on each variable and ignores the linear constraints, while forecast reconciliation enforces such constraints by using a single forecast per variable. To bridge this gap, we develop an original coherent forecast combination framework, in which the joint problem of combination across experts and coherence across variables is formulated as a linearly constrained optimization problem. Closed-form expressions are derived for the coherent combined forecast and its error covariance matrix, and the statistical properties of the resulting estimators are discussed. A Monte Carlo experiment and a forecasting application to an Australian daily electricity generation dataset confirm that the proposed approach significantly improves forecast accuracy with respect to standard forecast combination and reconciliation alternatives.

papers.title: Exchangeable Gaussian Processes with application to epidemics
papers.abstract: We develop a Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling collections of related epidemic trajectories using exchangeable Gaussian processes. The proposed formulation induces structured dependence across time-varying transmission processes through shared latent Gaussian process components, leading to interpretable pooling behaviour, variance decompositions and intra-class correlation parameters that quantify information sharing across populations. The framework accommodates both direct and indirect observation regimes, including noisy measurements of effective reproduction numbers, latent transmission models for Chikungunya outbreaks and age-structured epidemic systems driven by partially observed infection dynamics. We discuss connections with broader multi-output Gaussian process formulations, including coregionalisation and latent factor models, while emphasising the interpretation of the proposed approach as a functional random-effects framework for related temporal trajectories. A simulation study investigates the behaviour of the proposed models under varying cross-population dependence structures including dependent, weakly dependent and independent settings. Across several epidemic applications, the proposed models demonstrate strong predictive performance while providing interpretable insights into shared and population-specific transmission dynamics.

papers.title: Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation for a Genuinely Unbalanced Dynamic Network Panel Data Model
papers.abstract: This paper develops quasi-maximum likelihood estimation for genuinely unbalanced dynamic network panel data models. We first study a baseline one-way fixed effect specification and then extend the framework to two-way fixed effects. The model accommodates contemporaneous and lagged network spillovers, temporal dependence, and a listing effect that operates when a unit first appears in the panel. For the baseline specification, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the QMLE, characterize the incidental-parameter bias, and propose a bias-corrected estimator. We further provide a consistent estimator of the asymptotic covariance matrix, to enable feasible inference. Under the two-way fixed effect extension, we derive the corresponding asymptotic distribution, bias correction, and covariance matrix estimator, accounting for the additional bias component induced by the time fixed effects. Monte Carlo simulations examine the finite sample performance of the proposed estimators and inference procedure. An empirical application to Airbnb listings from New Zealand and New York City reveals region-specific patterns in spatial and temporal price transmission, highlighting the importance of modeling genuine unbalancedness in dynamic network settings.

papers.title: Assessment of evidence against homogeneity in exhaustive subgroup treatment effect plots
papers.abstract: Exhaustive subgroup treatment effect plots are constructed by displaying all subgroup treatment effects of interest against subgroup sample size, providing a useful overview of the observed treatment effect heterogeneity in a clinical trial. As in any exploratory subgroup analysis, however, the observed estimates suffer from small sample sizes and multiplicity issues. To facilitate more interpretable exploratory assessments, this paper introduces a computationally efficient method to generate homogeneity regions within exhaustive subgroup treatment effect plots. Using the Doubly Robust (DR) learner, pseudo-outcomes are used to estimate subgroup effects and derive reference distributions, quantifying how surprising observed heterogeneity is under a homogeneous effects model. Explicit formulas are derived for the homogeneity region and different methods for calculation of the critical values are compared. The method is illustrated with a cardiovascular trial and evaluated via simulation, showing well-calibrated inference and improved performance over standard approaches using simple differences of observed group means.

papers.title: Competing Risk Analysis in Cardiovascular Outcome Trials: A Simulation Comparison of Cox and Fine-Gray Models
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular outcome trials commonly face competing risks when non-CV death prevents observation of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). While Cox proportional hazards models treat competing events as independent censoring, Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models explicitly handle competing risks, targeting different estimands. This simulation study using bivariate copula models systematically varies competing event rates (0.5%-5% annually), treatment effects on competing events (50% reduction to 50% increase), and correlation structures to compare these approaches. At competing event rates typical of CV outcome trials (~1% annually), Cox and Fine-Gray produce nearly identical hazard ratio estimates regardless of correlation strength or treatment effect direction. Substantial divergence occurs only with high competing rates and directionally discordant treatment effects, though neither estimator provides unbiased estimates of true marginal hazard ratios under these conditions. In typical CV trial settings with low competing event rates, Cox models remain appropriate for primary analysis due to superior interpretability. Pre-specified Cox models should not be abandoned for competing risk methods. Importantly, Fine-Gray models do not constitute proper sensitivity analyses to Cox models per ICH E9(R1), as they target different estimands rather than testing assumptions. As supplementary analysis, cumulative incidence using Aalen-Johansen estimator can provide transparency about competing risk impact. Under high competing-risk scenarios, alternative approaches such as inverse probability of censoring weighting, multiple imputation, or inclusion of all-cause mortality in primary endpoints warrant consideration.

papers.title: Anchors Away: Navigating Single-Arm Indirect Comparisons with Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression (ML-UMR-SA)
papers.abstract: Unanchored indirect treatment comparisons using single-arm evidence are increasingly used in health technology assessment (HTA) when anchored comparisons of randomized evidence are not possible. Existing population-adjusted methods, including matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) and simulated treatment comparison (STC), are generally limited to pairwise analyses and typically estimate marginal effects in the comparator study population, which may differ from the decision-relevant target population. We propose multilevel unanchored meta-regression for single-arm indirect comparisons (ML-UMR-SA), a Bayesian outcome-regression framework for synthesizing individual patient data and aggregate data from single-arm evidence. ML-UMR-SA respecifies multilevel network meta-regression to pool absolute outcomes rather than relative treatment effects, jointly modeling individual- and aggregate-level data and linking aggregate outcomes through marginalization over study-specific covariate distributions, enabling estimation across multiple treatments, studies, and target populations. ML-UMR-SA distinguishes assumptions required to identify treatment effects from those required to transport results to target populations. Valid inference relies on strong and often unverifiable assumptions, particularly conditional constancy of absolute effects and cross-treatment identifying assumptions such as the shared prognostic factor assumption (SPFA). These requirements are made explicit within a Bayesian modeling framework that facilitates sensitivity analyses. In simulations without unobserved confounding, ML-UMR-SA produced low bias and nominal coverage for comparator-population effects. Transportability to alternative populations depended critically on identifying assumptions, whereas incorporating subgroup information restored near-unbiased estimation and nominal coverage.

papers.title: Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging for uncertainty quantification of electricity price forecasts
papers.abstract: Quantifying the uncertainty of forecasting models is essential to assess and mitigate the risks associated with data-driven decisions, especially in volatile domains such as electricity markets. In this paper, we propose a computationally efficient isotonic variant of Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA), called Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging (iQRA), for generating probabilistic forecasts from ensembles of point forecasts. Building on QRA, we introduce stochastic order constraints as a hyperparameter-free regularization mechanism that reduces computational complexity while maintaining competitive forecast accuracy. We further demonstrate that the same isotonic regularization principle can be applied to the smoothed estimator of QRA. In an extensive forecasting study of two European day-ahead electricity markets, we show that iQRA and its smoothed variant consistently rank among the top state-of-the-art postprocessing methods in terms of reliability and sharpness. It produces well-calibrated prediction intervals, with smoothed iQRA providing superior reliability even when compared against coverage-oriented conformal prediction. We further introduce a battery arbitrage evaluation, showing that the leading probabilistic methods achieve the highest profit per trade and that probabilistic risk control improves the economic value of trading decisions. Isotonic regularization offers a scalable hyperparameter-free variable selection for linear quantile regression, making iQRA attractive for practical decision-support systems in energy markets.

papers.title: Hurricane recovery gaps lie in reconnection, not local restart
papers.abstract: Climate-intensified hurricanes disrupt urban mobility, yet whether recovery is equitable across the rural-urban gradient is unclear. Analyzing device-based mobility for Hurricanes Helene and Milton, we find local activity restarted within approximately 4.5 days in both storms, whereas reconnection to the outside world took 5 days in coastal-urban Florida but 11 in inland-rural Appalachia. The gap lies in external reconnection, not local restart, implying planners should target rural isolation.

papers.title: Multi-fidelity Gaussian process regression for noisy outputs and non-nested experimental designs: decoupled versus joint likelihood optimization
papers.abstract: This paper investigates a recursive formulation of auto-regressive multi-fidelity Gaussian process regression in the challenging setting of noisy and non-nested high- and low-fidelity data. We propose a decoupled optimization strategy based on the expectation-maximization algorithm, which exploits the structure of the recursive model. In particular, we derive closed-form update formulas when the scaling factor is modeled as a parametric linear predictor. This approach is compared with the fully coupled likelihood maximization of the classical, non-recursive formulation. A series of benchmark experiments, covering applications of increasing complexity, highlights the performance of both approaches. The results demonstrate that the proposed recursive strategy substantially reduces training time when large low-fidelity datasets are available, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy and uncertainty estimation.
